idiom_name: typed component contract + dynamic import() with runtime shape validation
implementation_notes: TypeScript contributes the contract, not the mechanism: components are typed by a Component interface imported from a shared package and the configuration can be typed (satisfies ComponentConfig) so a typo is a compile error, while the runtime step remains await import(specifier) exactly as in JavaScript. Because types are erased, the configurator must still validate the loaded module's shape at the boundary (a factory check, a schema or an exported contract version) - a separately compiled component's types were never checked against yours. Bundlers turn literal dynamic imports into chunks or lazy edges; for a directory of components use a statically analysable glob (Vite import.meta.glob, webpack require.context), since variable specifiers are invisible to the build.
pitfalls: Erased types: a component built against an older contract still compiles in its own project, so only a runtime shape or version check at the link step catches the mismatch - TypeScript cannot verify a separately compiled component.

A computed import() specifier is opaque to bundlers, and moduleResolution/module settings (NodeNext vs bundler) decide whether the configured specifier resolves at all - extension-carrying ESM paths, package exports maps and import attributes are the usual production-only failures.

Global declaration merging or ambient .d.ts augmentation of the contract can make component types visible everywhere and silently change what the host thinks it loads; keep the contract a normal exported module and pin its version.
